Hi everyone,

I'm excited to share a project I've been working on: xeus-lean https://github.com/Verilean/xeus-lean

It is a Jupyter kernel for Lean 4 based on the xeus protocol. The key characteristic of this implementation is that the main loop and kernel logic are implemented in Lean 4 itself (binding to xeus via FFI), rather than wrapping Lean from C++.

This serves as a proof-of-concept for:

  1. Using Lean 4 for system-level programming and complex C++ interoperability.
  2. Creating interactive environments purely within the Lean ecosystem.

Future Roadmap: My ultimate goal involves compiling this kernel to WebAssembly (WASM). This would enable Lean 4 to run entirely in the browser via JupyterLite, providing a zero-setup, interactive learning environment for tutorials and textbooks without backend servers.

I hope this helps anyone looking to run Lean 4 in Jupyter notebooks. Feedback and contributions are welcome!

Good job with that! :smiley:

Hi, just wanted to ask, are you still planning to try and compile your kernel to WASM? I have a use for this in order to pre-check proofs client-side before being submitted for server-side verification. Looking at the Kernel Arena I have concluded that the only kernel that is fully complete is the official one, but I'm not sure which C++ files to compile. If it contains external libraries such as for BigNum I'd either have to get the source for these too or reimplement them. Or if it's too hard I might be forced to go with a different proof system. But my preference is Lean. Any tips?

Hi, WASM has been supported for a month now.
IIRC, This docker file https://github.com/Verilean/xeus-lean/blob/main/Dockerfile.wasm should work with c++ files.

I believe it requires a few hacks.
https://github.com/Verilean/xeus-lean/blob/main/WASM_BUILD.md
Lean4 is multithreaded, but Wasm is single-threaded. Adjustments were needed in that regard, so a patch was applied.
I had started working on other tasks while I was planning to set up CI and upload it to GitHub Pages.
Patching the lean4 runtime would make WASM support much easier.

While multithreading is supported, enabling it introduces another issue: it requires cross-origin headers, making deployment more complicated.
https://web.dev/articles/webassembly-threads

Hello, I was able to confirm today that the wasm kernel works in a browser.
https://verilean.github.io/xeus-lean/lab/index.html
I'd love to run a wasm-based LSP in the browser, do you know if the xlean.js/xlean.wasm artifacts would be usable as-is, or would we need to untangle the build process a bit for that?

Short answer: xlean.wasm can't be used as-is for LSP, but the runtime foundation is reusable.

The WASM binary includes a patched single-threaded Lean 4 runtime with Init.oleans, but Lean.Server.* modules aren't compiled in. To get LSP in the browser, one approach is running a separate lean-lsp.wasm in a second Web Worker (no SharedArrayBuffer needed, works on GitHub Pages). The main challenges are build complexity and binary size — adding Server + Std + Lean.oleans could push it to 1-2GB.

A more incremental path: we're planning to add complete_request and inspect_request to the Jupyter kernel protocol, using InfoTree data that's already available in the REPL. That would give tab-completion and hover info in JupyterLab without a full LSP. Not the same as a standalone LSP server, but covers the most useful features.

If you're interested in the full WASM LSP direction, happy to discuss the build changes needed — the runtime patches for single-threaded WASM are the hard part and those are already done.
Thanks! Getting this done is not my main focus right now, so I hope to cycle back to this at some point in the future:)

Added loading functionality for the Std and Lean packages. The compression of package files reduced the file size to just 260MB.
It might work for basic proofs and functional programming tutorials.
https://verilean.github.io/xeus-lean/lab/index.html

Hello! I wanted to share a new tutorial I created for learning functional programming with Lean, powered by JupyterLite.

The content is maintained as a base Markdown file, which is then converted into a static site page and a Jupyter notebook using the xlean-convert CLI.

Here is the link: https://verilean.github.io/xeus-lean/tutorial/ I'd love to hear your thoughts!

Cool project! I tried that tutorial on JupyterLite and it seems to work pretty well, although sometimes cells randomly take a long time to run. Also, what's the expected memory usage of xeus-lean in JupyterLite? For one notebook open it's around 5.3GB for me, and balloons up to 11GB if I open multiple notebooks at the same time.

@Asei Inoue Thx!
@Anthony Wang
Thank you for your feedback. I reduced the memory usage to the half size on the wasm runtime.

The first wasm kernel boots in 30 seconds, but the second kernel is ready in less than 5 seconds.
Data is cached in indexeddb for faster startup.
Loading and executing mathlib is also possible, but it's not very smooth because it writes about 2GB to indexeddb.
It should be sufficient for doing the lean tutorial, though.
https://verilean.github.io/xeus-lean/lab/index.html

Generally, it's best to run mathlib on a native kernel. MCP Server functionality has also been added, allowing you to control the notebook from the claude code.
